lesson.title: The Middle Ground: Polar Covalent Bonds
lesson.summary: Polar covalent bonds sit between equal sharing and full ionic transfer, with electrons genuinely shared between two atoms but pulled noticeably closer to whichever one is more electronegative.
lesson.body:
Polar covalent bonds occupy the middle stretch of the electronegativity difference scale, roughly delta EN 0.4 to 1.7 under the common guideline. What defines this middle ground is that real sharing of the electron pair is still happening, unlike an ionic bond where the more electronegative atom has essentially taken full possession of the electron, but that sharing is noticeably unequal, unlike a nonpolar covalent bond where the two atoms split the electron density almost exactly evenly. A polar covalent bond is, in a real sense, a covalent bond with a small amount of ionic character mixed in.

Chemists represent this unequal sharing with the same delta plus and delta minus labels introduced with bond polarity, and often draw an arrow along the bond pointing from the delta plus end toward the delta minus end, that is, toward the more electronegative atom, to show the direction the electron density has shifted. This arrow is the bond dipole, and its direction and approximate size are exactly what you need to track when several polar bonds around one central atom are added together to judge a whole molecule's polarity.

Water's O-H bonds are a strong worked example. Oxygen's electronegativity of about 3.44 compared to hydrogen's 2.20 gives a delta EN of about 1.24, clearly inside the polar covalent range. Each O-H bond in water is written as O delta minus, H delta plus, with the shared electrons pulled noticeably toward oxygen, and this individual bond polarity is one half of the reason water behaves the way it does as a solvent.

Ammonia's N-H bonds sit in the same category but with a smaller gap. Nitrogen's electronegativity of about 3.04 against hydrogen's 2.20 gives a delta EN of about 0.84, still polar covalent, but less strongly polarized than the O-H bond in water. This kind of comparison, checking where a bond falls within the polar covalent range rather than just whether it clears the 0.4 cutoff, is often more useful than the category label alone.

Carbon-oxygen bonds offer another common polar covalent example, and one that shows up constantly in organic chemistry. With oxygen at about 3.44 and carbon at about 2.55, a C-O bond has a delta EN of about 0.89, placing it clearly in the polar covalent range, similar in strength to the C=O bond dipole found in formaldehyde. Recognizing that a bond is polar covalent this way, from its atoms and their delta EN alone, is the first of two steps needed before you can say anything about whether the whole molecule containing that bond is polar.

Having polar bonds is necessary but not, by itself, sufficient to predict whether an entire molecule is polar. Whether the individual bond dipoles in a molecule add up to a meaningful net dipole, or cancel each other out by symmetry, depends on molecular geometry as much as on the bonds themselves. That interaction between bond polarity and molecular shape is exactly the subject of dipole moment, the concept that follows directly from this one.
